acquisition.why: Pure SEO/AI-search inbound; agents can do keyword research and publish content, though ranking is slow and Google-dependent.

onboarding.why: No onboarding; users land and use the tool.

billing.why: AdSense/Ezoic pay automatically; no customer billing.

support.why: Minimal; occasional bug reports and data refreshes (e.g. UK tax rates yearly) an agent can draft.

scores.R_why: Very cheap to build (domain + hosting well under £300), fits 6-8 h/week, and Ricardo's technical skill helps. UK-specific calculators (tax, stamp duty, student loan) are a natural niche. Cookie consent (CMP) is needed for ads, and email gating needs PECR consent. Revenue is small until traffic is large: about £20-80/month per 10k page views [E].
scores.M_why: Calculator SERPs are saturated, and Google AI Overviews and LLMs answer many simple calculations directly. Copying is trivial, and one first-hand claim (build time) says nothing about revenue. Long-tail UK niches still have some room.
scores.one_line: Almost fully automatable and cheap to test as a portfolio of UK-niche calculators, but AI answers and saturation squeeze traffic, so expect pocket money, not a business [E].

acquisition.why: Paid Reddit/Facebook ads and app-store/SEO are legal inbound. Agents can run creative and bidding, but ad spend needs human approval and CAC is untested.

delivery.why: Software; agents can handle feature tweaks and maintenance with occasional human review.

support.why: Consumer hobbyists send feature requests and bug reports; agents can triage most of them.

scores.R_why: Ricardo can build an app cheaply. But £300 buys little paid-ad testing, $10-20/month for a tracker is ambitious, and churn among hobbyists is likely. UK hobby communities exist but are small; app-store review and posting rules add friction.
scores.M_why: Free incumbents exist (BG Stats, garden planners, golf apps like 18Birdies) and vibe-coded clones are multiplying. Willingness to pay is unproven, and there are no first-hand claims.
scores.one_line: Agent-friendly SaaS shape, but the pitch is a hypothetical brainstorm with strong free competitors and an unproven $10-20/month price for hobby trackers.

acquisition.why: Programmatic SEO plus being cited by ChatGPT; agents generate and publish pages. Exposed to Google helpful-content updates.

delivery.why: AI recipe generator via API plus auto-generated pages; needs occasional quality and brand-name checks.

support.why: Low-ticket consumer queries and refunds an agent can handle.

scores.R_why: Technically easy for Ricardo and tools cost about $50/month, within budget. But SEO feedback takes about 5 months. Using restaurant brand names carries UK trademark and passing-off sensitivity, and AI-content penalties are a risk. The claimed $700-800/month suggests a modest ceiling.
scores.M_why: Recipe search is among the most AI-disrupted SERPs (AI Overviews, ChatGPT recipes), copycat-recipe sites are plentiful, and the app's launch spike is not repeatable. A single source, though first-hand.
scores.one_line: A credible first-hand, agent-runnable pSEO model, but the revenue is small, recipe SEO is crowded and AI-eroded, and brand-name pages carry legal risk.

acquisition.why: Build-in-public content on X and a newsletter. Agents can draft research posts, but audience growth needs an authentic voice and human approval.

delivery.why: Scraping and analysis software plus AI-written reports; scrapers break and need upkeep.

support.why: Developer users ask technical questions; agents can answer most of them.

scores.R_why: Ricardo has the technical ability, but building an audience is slow at 6-8 h/week. Marketplace scraping terms (Apple, Shopify, etc.) are a risk, and the host himself doubts each marketplace is big enough for a tool.
scores.M_why: ASO tools (AppTweak, Sensor Tower, Astro) are established, and indie-dev audience content is crowded. One speculative mention with no claims.
scores.one_line: An idea pitched with no evidence, in a crowded ASO tool space, behind a slow audience-building moat that is hard to delegate to agents.

acquisition.why: Sales depend on an existing audience or author platform. Amazon KDP ads and SEO are inbound, but without an audience discovery is weak.

onboarding.why: Readers just buy on Amazon or a store.

delivery.why: Credible nonfiction needs the author's expertise and voice over months. AI drafting helps, but quality and authority need heavy human involvement, and AI-slop books get flagged on KDP.

billing.why: KDP and publishers pay royalties automatically.

scores.R_why: An 18-22 month project at 6-8 h/week, and the big outcomes ($500k advance, $1M launch) rely on huge existing audiences Ricardo lacks. KDP royalty income is typically low for unknown authors [E].
scores.M_why: KDP is flooded with AI-generated nonfiction and Amazon now caps uploads. Books work as authority for other offers, not as a standalone income source.
scores.one_line: Well evidenced as an authority play for people who already have big audiences, but not an agent-run income source for an unknown part-timer in a flooded KDP market.

acquisition.why: Etsy search and paid social are legal inbound. Etsy is the main channel but platform-dependent, and agents can manage listings.

onboarding.why: The customer uploads photos and details via form or Etsy messages; occasional clarifications are needed.

delivery.why: AI generation plus print-on-demand fulfilment; outputs need a quality check, especially of children's likenesses, and physical print issues occur.

support.why: Gift buyers raise delivery, reprint and likeness complaints; agents handle most with escalation.

scores.R_why: Cheap to test on Etsy UK with UK print-on-demand for well under £300. Seasonal gift demand exists. Children's photos are personal data under UK GDPR and need care. Consumer refund rules for personalised goods are favourable.
scores.M_why: A crowded personalised-book market (Wonderbly, many Etsy sellers), and ChatGPT lets buyers DIY. Sam himself sees a 3-4 year window.
scores.one_line: An Etsy plus print-on-demand gift product that agents can mostly run, but margins and differentiation are thin as buyers can DIY with ChatGPT and incumbents dominate.

acquisition.why: B2B cold email to company marketers with a free sample ebook is PECR-OK, and agents can find leads via Apollo and draft emails. Avoid LinkedIn DM automation (against platform terms).

onboarding.why: B2B clients need scoping, branding assets and approvals; agents can run intake forms with human sign-off.

delivery.why: Transcript to ebook, blog and LinkedIn posts is very agent-friendly, with a human quality pass on brand voice.

support.why: Revision requests and account management; agents draft, the human approves.

scores.R_why: Fits Ricardo's skills and budget (Apollo free tier, Claude). UK B2B webinar culture is strong. But $1-8k pricing is aspirational, B2B sales cycles are slow, and a human must stand behind the client relationship.
scores.M_why: Repurposing is heavily commoditised (Descript, Castmagic, in-house ChatGPT), and the agency space is crowded. The cold-email free-sample angle gives some edge.
scores.one_line: A legal B2B cold-email service where AI does most delivery, but clients can increasingly DIY. Pricing claims are pitches, not first-hand results, so test with UK SaaS webinar hosts [E].

acquisition.why: Needs SEO or paid ads for 'infographic CV'. No channel was identified, and $5 pricing can't support paid acquisition.

delivery.why: Image or HTML generation via API; errors in AI-rendered text need guardrails.

support.why: Revision and refund requests over garbled output.

scores.R_why: Easy for Ricardo to build. But at $5 it needs volume, UK recruiters and ATS systems disfavour infographic CVs, and CVs are personal data under UK GDPR. Demand is unvalidated.
scores.M_why: Canva templates, free AI CV builders and ChatGPT do this already. The ATS-unfriendly format limits demand. Purely hypothetical claims.
scores.one_line: A trivially automatable but hypothetical, low-price product that free tools already cover, with a format UK hiring systems penalise.
